title: Muslims in Britain
hook: a dome in Woking, a terraced house in Liverpool, sailors by the docks in Cardiff

segments.voice: Yesterday, enslaved African Muslims, people like Omar ibn Said who kept their faith far from home and wrote it down in Arabic. Your line was: they prayed in chains. Whose name did you carry with you? Day one thousand twenty-seven.

A domed mosque sits behind the trees in Woking, a quiet commuter town south of London. It is named for a woman far away, Shah Jahan, the Begum of Bhopal in India, who helped pay for it. Up north in Liverpool, a local solicitor named William Quilliam becomes Muslim, takes the name Abdullah, and opens a mosque in a row of ordinary terraced houses. Down in Cardiff, near the docks, sailors from Yemen and Somalia rent rooms, marry, raise children, and set aside a room to pray. No palace in any of it. Just streets, rain and neighbors. Today: Muslims in Britain.
screen: `A DOME IN WOKING.` → `A TERRACED HOUSE IN LIVERPOOL.` → `SAILORS BY THE CARDIFF DOCKS.`

segments.voice: Here is the one idea for today: Muslims in Britain are not a single arrival. They are many threads, woven over a long time. Some threads are converts, like Abdullah Quilliam in Liverpool. Some are sailors and dock workers, from Yemen, Somalia and the Indian subcontinent, who settled in port towns. Some are soldiers from India who fought in Britain's wars; near that mosque in Woking there is a burial ground made for Muslim soldiers. And then came families, from Pakistan, Bangladesh, India and later from Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans, who came to work in mills, factories, hospitals and buses, and stayed. You can read that history in the buildings. Some mosques were built from the ground up with domes and minarets. Others began as a front room, a shop, a warehouse or an old chapel. On Brick Lane in East London stands a building that was put up as a chapel for French Protestant refugees, later served as a synagogue for Jewish families, and is now a mosque. One building, three faiths, each praying in turn under the same roof. The Qur'an has a line that fits a faith carried to a cold, rainy island: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." For British Muslims, that has meant praying in a Cardiff boarding house, a Bradford mill, a Woking garden. The faith did not wait for the perfect place. It found a corner, faced Mecca, and began.
screen: `NOT ONE ARRIVAL, MANY THREADS.` · `CONVERTS, SAILORS, SOLDIERS, FAMILIES.` · `ONE BUILDING, THREE FAITHS.` · `EAST AND WEST BELONG TO GOD.` · then, large: `A LONG BRITISH STORY.`

segments.voice: The practice: get to know your local mosque's history, starting with what you already know. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the mosque nearest where you live, or one you pass on the way to work. What was the building before? Who prayed there first? How did they find the money, the land, the patience? If you don't know, notice that, and keep the question for later. Then think of the first handful of people who unrolled their prayer mats in that place. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for them in your own words. If not, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Muslims in Britain. Converts, sailors, soldiers and families, praying in front rooms, chapels and domed mosques. Today's word.
Your line: a long british story. Today, look up one fact about the mosque nearest you: when it opened, or what the building was before. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

howItsDone: British Muslims pray in a wide range of buildings, from purpose-built mosques to converted houses, shops and chapels, and some local mosques keep and share the history of the people who founded them.
